title: Dry bread and cool water
hookLine: eat your dry bread, drink cool water, and don't envy another's buttered bread (Farid salok, ang 1379)

lines: A BOX FROM THE GOOD PLACE.
cards: Lunch at your desk: a sandwich from home, a bit squashed, perfectly fine. Then someone across the room opens a box from the good place down the street, and the smell reaches you. The sandwich hasn't changed.
It's exactly as good as it was a minute ago. Does it still taste the same? Farid has a pair of couplets about exactly this moment, and they're about bread.

teach.h: MY BREAD IS WOOD; HUNGER IS MY RELISH.
teach.b: Both couplets sit together on Ang 1379. The first, in paraphrase: Farid, my bread is made of wood, and hunger is my relish. Those who eat buttered bread will suffer much pain.

Tradition says Farid carried a piece of wood shaped like bread and held it when hunger came, as a discipline. Whatever the story, the line is clear about where the taste comes from: hunger is the seasoning.
Then the second, today's couplet. In paraphrase: eat your dry, plain bread and drink cool water. Farid, don't look at someone else's buttered bread and let your heart long for it.
Look at what Farid isn't saying.
Not that butter is wicked, or that the hungry should be glad to be hungry. Sikh teaching, after all, builds a free kitchen, langar, where everyone is fed. Going hungry is not the goal.
The target is narrower: the looking. Dekh, see, and tarsaae, to long, to ache for.

teach.h: THE EYES GO TO ANOTHER'S PLATE.
teach.b: The trouble starts when the eyes cross the room to another person's plate, and your own bread suddenly tastes of less.
The Punjabi pair for the plain food is rukhi sukhi: dry and simple, ordinary meals in ordinary homes. Beside it, cool water, not a luxury, but on a hot day, a real gift.
What's in front of you is enough, if you stop measuring it against someone else's. Envy adds nothing to the other plate. It only takes something from yours.

how: Farid's saloks are read and sung in gurdwaras with the rest of Gurbani; Sikhs read this couplet as a teaching against envy and greed, alongside the langar, the free kitchen where everyone eats the same simple food together.

o: a sweet bread baked only for festivals
buttered bread from a rich man's table
dry, plain bread, eaten without envy

games.q: inside the couplets — tap the pairs.

s: Farid says butter itself is wicked
the couplet's target is the longing look at someone else's plate.
in the couplet, hunger is the relish
my bread is made of wood, and hunger is my relish.
Sikh teaching praises making people go without
Sikhs keep langar, a free kitchen where everyone is fed.

games.q: you're eating dry bread with cool water. across the way, someone opens buttered bread. what does Farid say to do?
o: eat yours, drink the water, and don't let your heart long for theirs.
throw yours away and go without.
games.why: eat your dry bread and drink cool water, Farid says; don't look at another's buttered bread and let your heart long for it.

practice: If something plain is nearby, a piece of bread, a cracker, a glass of water, take one slow bite or one slow sip and taste it all the way through.
When the mind wanders to something better, or to something someone else has, notice it and come back to this taste. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Rukhi sukhi. Farid's Punjabi words for dry and plain bread: eat what's in front of you, and don't long for someone else's buttered bread.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: dry and plain, Farid's words for simple bread.

carryVoice: Your line: dry bread is enough. Hunger is the seasoning. Day seven hundred sixty-four, done.

sources.ref: Salok Sheikh Farid (roti meri kaath ki; rukhi sukhi khaae kai), Ang 1379
